name: Standing desk / riser

lead: A standing desk or riser lifts the keyboard and monitor so you can work on your feet or switch between sitting and standing. People use it to cut hours of slumped sitting, which they associate with a rounded-shoulder, forward-head look.

Standing reduces sitting time and varies posture, and changing positions through the day is commonly described as mattering more than any one posture. A Cochrane review found sit-stand desks reduced sitting at work by roughly one and a half to two hours, with low-quality evidence and little data on health outcomes. No study has tested whether a standing desk changes visible posture.

paras: Users alternate between sitting and standing through the day using electric sit-stand desks, crank desks or tabletop risers, with the screen at eye level. It is often combined with movement breaks and back-strengthening work.
Long static standing causes foot, leg and back discomfort, and standing raises energy expenditure only slightly. A riser at the wrong height can strain the neck and wrists.

angle.text: Alternating sitting and standing breaks up long slouched stretches, so you carry yourself less hunched through the day. Sit-stand desks are studied for comfort and sitting time; effects on visible posture are user-reported.

lead: A standing desk is a work surface at a height suited to working on one's feet, or to sitting on a high stool. Variants include fixed-height desks, electric or crank-operated sit-stand desks that move between sitting and standing positions, and tabletop risers that sit on an existing desk and lift the keyboard and monitor. [1][2]

They are promoted as a way to reduce long periods of slumped sitting, which proponents associate with rounded shoulders and forward head posture. In research, standing desks have been studied mainly as a way to reduce sitting time and sedentary behaviour in offices and schools. [3][4][5]

Systematic and scoping reviews report that sit-stand desks reliably change behaviour, reducing sitting time, but that effects on measured health outcomes are small or inconsistent and long-term data are limited. A Cochrane review summary rates the evidence that desks reduce sitting at work as low quality. No study has tested whether a standing desk changes facial or skeletal appearance. [1][4][6]
infobox: Fixed standing desk, electric sit-stand desk, tabletop riser
Reduces sitting time; health effects small or unclear

paras: Standing desks have been built in many styles, including telephone desks and drafting tables. Height-adjustable designs raise and lower via an electric motor, hand crank or counterbalance. Because standing users move about more than seated ones, adjusting the user's height with a pedestal is impractical, so desks are either custom-made or adjustable. [1]
A desk riser is a platform that sits on top of an existing seated desk to bring the work surface to standing height; risers may be fixed or adjustable. [1]

Writers and statesmen including Thomas Jefferson, Charles Dickens, Winston Churchill, Ernest Hemingway, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Vladimir Nabokov are recorded as having worked standing, some at specially made desks or lecterns. [1] Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, additionally describes ancient and medieval lecterns and an adjustable desk made for Marie Antoinette in 1778; these details have not been checked against primary sources. [2]

Interest in sit-stand work revived with computer-based office work in the late twentieth century and with research on the health effects of prolonged sitting, and sit-stand desks have since been offered by many employers. [1][2]
Human studies on standing desks are numerous but mostly examine sedentary behaviour, discomfort and metabolic markers rather than posture appearance.

A Cochrane review of workplace interventions for reducing sitting found low-quality evidence that providing a sit-stand desk reduced sitting at work by roughly one and a half to two hours per day, with a smaller effect over longer follow-up. Wikipedia summarizes the range as 30 minutes to two hours. [1][6]

A 2019 scoping review of 53 articles on sit-stand desks in office workers found that 61 percent of behavioural results, 37 percent of physiological results, 7 percent of work performance results, 31 percent of psychological results, 43 percent of discomfort results and 18 percent of posture results were statistically significant. The authors concluded that desks effectively change behaviour but only mildly affect health outcomes, and that effects were strongest for discomfort and weakest for productivity. [4]

A 2015 systematic review of standing and treadmill desks found few physiological changes with standing desks, with treadmill desks showing larger improvements in glucose, HDL cholesterol and body measures, and mixed results for psychological well-being. [3]

A randomized crossover trial in 23 university students found that alternating sitting and standing every 30 minutes over two hours did not change postprandial glucose or insulin responses compared with continuous sitting. [7] Studies of vascular function in sedentary middle-aged adults have examined whether desk standing offsets sitting-induced endothelial dysfunction. [8] A 2019 report examined chronic standing desk use and arterial stiffness. [9]

A randomized trial of a low-cost standing desk in 41 office employees examined real-time affective states at work. [10] Another randomized trial asked whether people compensate for reduced sitting at work by sitting more elsewhere. [11] A pilot study examined stand-biased desks and sleep quality in high school students. [12]

A 2016 systematic review of eight classroom studies reported that standing time increased in all studies and sitting time fell by roughly 59 to 64 minutes where measured. [5] A 2025 scoping review mapped 17 studies of standing desks in university settings and noted sparse evidence. [13]
A 2014 systematic review of active workstations, including standing, treadmill and cycling desks, examined effects on health and work performance. [14]

Grokipedia reports that prolonged standing is associated with foot and lower back pain and with circulatory problems such as chronic venous insufficiency, and that large cohort studies find that more standing time does not lower cardiovascular risk; it cites these findings to prospective studies not independently checked here. [2] A 2018 paper on ergonomics and the standing desk discusses set-up considerations. [15]
Wikipedia notes there is no international consensus on recommended ratios of sitting and standing at work. [1]

In appearance and posture circles, standing desks and risers are presented as tools for avoiding hunched sitting. The published research measures sitting time and health markers; no study reports effects on forward head posture or facial appearance. [4]
